name: Jan
notable_features: A Tauri desktop app (Rust core, web front-end) with an OpenAI-compatible local server on localhost:1337, so other applications can use whatever Jan has loaded.
Backend variants are a first-class build concept: engine builds are selected with JAN_ENGINE_VARIANT from the tokens cpu, vulkan, metal, cuda12, cuda13, and hip/rocm, composable with '-'.
Ships an mlx-server component alongside the llama.cpp engine, so Apple Silicon has a native MLX path in addition to llama.cpp/Metal.
Custom assistants, MCP integration for agentic use, and cloud-provider connectors (OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Groq, MiniMax) alongside local models.
Available as Windows exe, macOS universal dmg, Linux deb and AppImage, plus Microsoft Store and Flathub.
hardware_caveats: The build-time engine variant is a real fork in the road: picking JAN_ENGINE_VARIANT=cpu gives you a CPU-only build and no GPU path at all. There is no runtime backend switching comparable to llama.cpp's --gpu flag across variants.

Windows build requires VS 2022 Build Tools (MSVC x64 workload + Windows SDK), LLVM, Ninja and CMake on PATH; the bundled llama.cpp engine builds with Ninja + clang-cl. The CUDA Toolkit is needed only for the cuda12/cuda13 variants.

Windows-specific build trap: an nvcc 'Could not open output file' error during the llama.cpp build means the build path crossed Windows' 260-character MAX_PATH limit, because nvcc does not honour the long-path opt-in. The build script relocates the engine build tree to %LOCALAPPDATA%\jan-engine automatically; if it still happens set JAN_ENGINE_BUILD_DIR to a short path or move the checkout closer to the drive root.
make dev must be run from Git Bash on Windows, since make dispatches recipes through sh — a plain cmd.exe will not work.
macOS 13.6+ required; the published minimum RAM guidance is 8GB for 3B models, 16GB for 7B and 32GB for 13B. Apple Silicon builds also need the MetalToolchain Xcode component.
Windows 10+ with GPU support for NVIDIA/AMD/Intel Arc is stated as the minimum for a decent experience, but the actual backend you get depends entirely on which engine variant was built.
best_for: A desktop ChatGPT replacement for a non-technical user who wants a GUI and a working download-and-go experience.
Apple Silicon users who want an app that uses MLX rather than only llama.cpp.
Offline, private use where cloud connectors are optional rather than the default.
Feeding a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint to other apps at localhost:1337.
Users who want assistants and MCP in one place instead of assembling separate tools.
avoid_for: Headless/server deployments — this is a desktop app with a sidecar server, not a serving stack.
Anyone needing to change backends at runtime; the backend is chosen at build time.
Benchmarking or performance work — Jan adds a desktop layer, not kernel speed.
Linux Arm64, which is documented only as a how-to issue link rather than a first-class release artifact.
notes: The engine-variant set (cpu, vulkan, metal, cuda12, cuda13, hip/rocm) is the most accurate description of Jan's real backend matrix, so supported_backends reflects that rather than a claim that all are present in any one build. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION while the README states Apache 2.0; recorded as Apache-2.0 per the project's own statement, with the discrepancy noted. Jan is a UI layer over llama.cpp plus MLX; the kernel-level backend detail belongs to the llama.cpp and MLX records.
